rv.q: Especially in its latter half, “Bimbo” traverses the gap between the very online and the very not online with exuberant intelligence.
Its humans are a lot less interesting than its god, but it relies on them to generate its plot.
The Last Bimbo of the Apocalypse is not only cutting-edge but it may presage the dawning of the next kind of musical – which may not be to all tastes.

The Last Bimbo of the Apocalypse may traffic in those Y2K aesthetics but there’s nothing old about this fresh and captivating new musical from the deliciously deranged minds of Michael Breslin and Patrick Foley, who brought us the now iconic and Pulitzer Prize nominated Circle Jerk.
Unapologetically campy, Last Bimbo is also stealthily brilliant, pulling back the curtain on the smoke-and-mirrors show that has overtaken much of our culture and politics.
Breslin and Foley’s one-act musical was made for and by the extremely online.
While The Last Bimbo of the Apocalypse is one curiously mixed-up musical, the production is sufficiently entertaining to amuse viewers willing to overlook its somewhat bipolar behavior.
The result is an unsatisfying production that is rarely visually arresting, even less often satirically insightful, and, when all is said and done, overtly tiresome.
Find out in this wacky, young, and insightful musical parody of the over-arching dominance of internet culture in our present times.
The Last Bimbo of the Apocalypse transforms yesterday's tabloid into an excavation of celebrity obsession and Gen Z social media-fueled social anxiety.
Unfortunately, Breslin’s book, co-written with Patrick Foley, has all the charm of an undisciplined child.

The cast is an exuberant delight, highlighted by Tony winner Shapiro (Matilda the Musical, You’re a Good Man, Charlie Brown) and Fuller (Six, Jagged Little Pill), who embody the loneliness that comes with online addiction.

cn.t: Critics find this Gen Z internet mystery musical about Y2K celebrity culture energetically unhinged and inventive, though some older reviewers dismiss it as too niche for those not extremely online.
